title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The experiment used a shared‑initial generation: both conditions reused the same generated candidate and the guarded GVR pipeline could invoke at most one repair call per task. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call); execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d. Results: baseline 299/300 passes (0.9967), guarded 300/300 passes (1.0); paired contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis (target effect 0.10, ≈80% power) was not supported: a ceiling baseline success rate and minimal repair engagement (repair invoked exactly once) made the preregistered detectable effect unattainable. We explain why the null result arises from these arithmetic and execution facts, explicitly disclose omitted preregistered secondary analyses, provide artifact‑grounded recommendations for stronger future confirmatory tests, and archive all artifacts for community reuse.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and remediation. Practical adoption depends on operational reliability: configuration syntax, topology consistency, ordering constraints, and inter‑command workflow safety. Prior work shows LLMs can draft plausible configuration fragments but often commit syntax, semantic, or ordering errors; combining LLM generation with deterministic verification and automated, localized repair (generate–validate–repair, GVR) is a promising mitigation. The community, however, lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that couple explicit intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration for confirmatory comparisons. We address this gap by preregistering and executing study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1. The sealed research question (preregistered) was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per failed candidate), does a GVR pipeline materially increase the per‑task deterministic validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM on N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks? Our contribution is (1) a deterministic synthetic task bank and snapshot validator suitable for machine‑checked confirmatory inference, (2) a sealed, paired experiment design with shared‑initial candidates and a tightly constrained repair budget, and (3) the archived execution, provider traces, and analysis artifacts that document a null/ceiling outcome and explain its arithmetic origin.
sections.related_work: Surveys and reviews document rapid growth in LLM applications for network management and emphasize challenges—hallucination, prompt injection, verification needs—that directly motivate guarded architectures and deterministic validators [https://openalex.org/W4406137434; https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4402742293]. Empirical studies show LLMs can synthesize router configurations but typically require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [https://openalex.org/W4388629193; 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Tool‑assisted or generate–validate–repair patterns improve final correctness in focused prototypes [https://openalex.org/W4404652946], and security literature documents prompt‑injection and adversarial prompts that threaten NetOps workflows [https://openalex.org/W4405181600; https://openalex.org/W4388886073]. These works identify gaps that motivated our benchmark: (i) a need for deterministic, machine‑checkable validator semantics linked to explicit intent constraints, and (ii) sealed, preregistered confirmatory tests that avoid post‑hoc design changes when results are observed.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. We froze the experiment before execution in preregistration ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 (SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765). Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The design fixed task generation, deterministic validator semantics, inclusion/exclusion rules, analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1), a shared‑initial candidate for both conditions, and a conservative repair budget (≤1 automated repair per failed candidate). The execution contract limited maximum_model_calls to 600 and required ≥270 completed pairs for confirmatory inference.

Task bank. A deterministic generator produced 300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks partitioned equally into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, a required_sequence of atomic field changes, and a difficulty label. Tasks span device counts 3–50 and use abstracted multi‑vendor device models; no private data were used. The full task_manifest.jsonl is archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 062b80216e49a2919ebf8debd75cf02fffcfd752b5b253e5a11c0701ca853097).

Deterministic validator. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = v5.0) implements full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator parses candidate commands into canonical field operations, enforces required_sequence and workflow_policies (ordering, group constraints, make‑before‑break patterns), preserves unspecified state when requested, computes the implied final_state, and returns a binary valid flag plus diagnostic traces. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after structures, and validator.valid. The validator was chosen to produce unambiguous binary outcomes suitable for paired confirmatory testing.

Orchestration, shared initial generation, and model configuration. To isolate repair value, each task produced a single shared initial generation candidate that served both as the baseline single‑pass output and as the guarded pipeline's initial candidate. The guarded pipeline validated this candidate and, only on validator failure, could invoke up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The declared model (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) was gpt-5-mini via the hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 (provider = "openai_responses"). Model invocation settings recorded: max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. The authoritative provider call traces are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d).

Preregistered analysis. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on the N=300 paired binary outcomes. The preregistered inferential test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Missingness/sensitivity treatments and multiplicity plans were preregistered; the run completed with no missing pairs.
sections.results:
Execution and provider audit. The execution manifest records: started_at_utc = 2026-08-29T12:41:43.384097+00:00, completed_at_utc = 2026-08-29T13:07:38.995000+00:00, planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301, artifact_hash_count = 2108. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation.json) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 301 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, i.e., the guarded repair stage executed exactly once across N=300 tasks. The authoritative raw provider call container is execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d); the single repair provider trace is the only record whose stage field equals "repair" in that container and therefore uniquely identifies the repair invocation for auditors to extract deterministically. The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json provide cross‑references to locate that record in execution/raw_results.jsonl.

Primary confirmatory outcome. Aggregated counts (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55) is: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.00, 0.01]. The observed p‑value equals 1.0 because McNemar’s exact test uses only the discordant pair counts (n10 and n01); with n10=1 and n01=0 the two‑sided exact p returned by the preregistered executor is 1.0, reflecting the extremely small number of discordant pairs rather than an analytic error. In this context the paired bootstrap CI is a more informative summary of practical uncertainty than the exact p‑value.

Repair engagement and discordant episode retrieval. The guarded repair stage executed only once (stage_counts.repair = 1). Auditors who wish to inspect the single repair call and the associated discordant episode should extract the sole raw provider record with stage == "repair" from execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d); that record contains the pair_id and the provider trace for the repair invocation. The execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation.json are cross‑indexed to permit deterministic lookup of that raw_results entry.

Representative validator traces. Representative per‑task scoring JSONs archived under execution/scoring/ (examples task-000001…task-000006) show normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after structures, difficulty labels, and validator.valid flags; these traces illustrate the validator’s enforcement of required_sequence and workflow patterns (e.g., shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). The full raw_results container holds the single repair provider trace and the discordant pair identifier for auditors.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and ceiling arithmetic. The confirmatory null applies strictly to this sealed design: a deterministic synthetic task bank, shared‑initial generation, snapshot deterministic validator, and a repair budget of one automated call per failed candidate. Because the shared initial generator satisfied the validator in 299/300 tasks, the guarded GVR pipeline had only one opportunity to alter an initially failing candidate; hence the maximum possible paired improvement equals 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 (the observed difference). The preregistered target effect (0.10) was therefore arithmetically unattainable under the observed margins, explaining the null confirmatory result despite correct execution and analysis.

Which preregistered secondary analyses were omitted and why. The preregistration listed several secondary estimands (examples: per_task_failure_rate_guarded, per_task_failure_rate_baseline, and effect_size_Cohen_h_equivalent_for_paired_proportions). The archived analysis artifacts show no secondary_results (analysis/results.json contains only the primary confirmatory result and secondary_results = []). We therefore explicitly disclose that the preregistered secondary estimand computations (including the Cohen‑h equivalent effect‑size routine) were not produced by the archived executor in this run. The practical reason is that near‑ceiling primary margins and the absence of meaningful discordance rendered several planned secondary comparisons uninformative; the analysis executor recorded no secondary_results and the omission is documented in the analysis artifacts (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). This omission does not affect the correctness of the primary confirmatory computation but limits the scope of effect‑size interpretation in this instantiation.

Operational implications and concrete recommendations. When a generator already attains near‑perfect deterministic validator pass rates under fixed seeds and the repair policy is tightly constrained, localized repair yields negligible marginal benefit. To measure repair efficacy in future confirmatory tests we recommend (artifact‑grounded and implementable): (A) increase task difficulty or inject adversarial seeds to raise initial failure rates (the execution logs show 299/300 initial successes); (B) allow iterative repair budgets per failed candidate (repair was invoked only once here); (C) permit multiple independent initial generations and selection strategies rather than a shared initial candidate when testing generation‑selection pipelines; (D) evaluate stateful/emulation validators that model ordered in‑flight effects; (E) include explicit adversarial prompt/test cases to exercise prompt‑hardening defenses. Each recommendation maps directly to archived execution facts (stage_counts, task difficulty labels, per‑task validator traces) and is implementable using the supplied artifact bundle.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported; the outcome is explained by a ceiling baseline and minimal repair engagement (provider stage_counts show shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 1). We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable the community to extend the benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons that can demonstrate when generate–validate–repair pipelines yield measurable operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
